title: The translation is not the Guru
word: The translation is not the Guru
hookLine: you look up the lyrics and still play the song; the English helps, so why read the Gurmukhi?
tomorrow: one page, opened each morning: who chooses it?

cards: A song in a language you don't speak gets stuck in your head. You look up the lyrics, read what they mean, and then go right back to playing the song. The meaning didn't replace it.
So here's yesterday's question, and it's a real one: if English helps, why read the Gurmukhi at all? Sikhs have two honest answers, and they don't fully agree.

teach.b: The first answer: sound first. For Sikhs, the Gurmukhi is the Guru's own word; a translation is an aid standing beside it. And the sound itself does something.
In the Japji, Guru Nanak gives whole verses to listening. In paraphrase: by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away; by listening, the devotees bloom.

teach.h: MEANING FIRST: REFLECT ON THE WORD.
teach.b: Not by understanding every word first. By listening. So you read the Gurmukhi, and let it work, and the meaning grows into it.
The second answer: meaning first. The Gurus' hymns keep calling for reflection on the Word, and Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that learning reflected on makes a person a help to others.

If the words never reach your understanding, how do they reach your life? For many people, a translation is the honest first step, and the sound follows once the meaning has a home. Here's where the two meet.
Neither side calls the translation the Guru. Both want the Gurmukhi heard and understood in the end.
The disagreement is about which comes first, and Sikhs live both: a grandmother who knows every sound by heart, a teenager reading the English underneath.
Today's line takes the first side's order, sound first, without dropping the second side's point: the sound is meant to be understood.

how: Sikhs honor the Gurmukhi text of the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru and treat translations as aids; some begin with the sound and let understanding grow, others begin with a translation and move toward reading the Gurmukhi.

games.q: what does “the translation is not the guru” mean?
o: a translation counts once a Guru approves it
the Guru wrote nothing down in any language
the Gurmukhi is the Guru; a translation only helps

p: by listening, sorrow is wiped away
honored as the Guru's own word

s: Sikhs treat a good translation of the Granth as the Guru
the Gurmukhi is honored as the Guru; every translation is an aid.
the Japji gives whole verses to listening
in paraphrase: by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away.
Sikhs all agree on whether sound or meaning comes first
both views are lived; they agree the translation is an aid, not the Guru.

games.q: a friend says: if i can't understand Gurmukhi, reading it is just noise, so why not English only? you lean her way. what's the best case for sound first?
o: the Japji says listening itself wipes sorrow away; the Gurmukhi is the Guru, and meaning grows into the sound.
Gurmukhi is simply more correct than English, so English readers are doing it wrong.
nobody needs to understand Gurbani at all; meaning was never the point.
games.why: the strongest case for sound first isn't that meaning doesn't matter. it's that the Guru's word works through listening, and understanding grows into it.

practice: Take one line you know a little, the Japji's opening if nothing else. Say the Gurmukhi sound out loud first, slowly, without looking at any English.
Then read the English once, and say the Gurmukhi again, and hear whether it sounds different now that you know a little of what it holds.

wordCard.voice: The translation is not the Guru: the Gurmukhi words are honored as the Guru; every translation, however good, is an aid beside them. The twelfth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Gurbani, the Guru's word, honored as the Guru; translations stand beside it.

carryVoice: Your line: sound first. Then let the meaning find its home in it. That's twelve.

sources.ref: Japji, pauris 8–11 (Ang 2–3, Guru Nanak: suniai… suniai dukh paap ka naas), paraphrased
Ang 356 (Raag Asa, Guru Nanak: vidya veechaaree taan parupkaaree), paraphrased
